name: Purple Tourmaline (Siberite)
spiritual: Connects the Crown to calm clarity
physical: Crystal healers link it to restful sleep
Many people keep it nearby for comfort during tension headaches
summary: Purple Tourmaline, known as Siberite, is a rare violet elbaite linked in crystal lore to intuition, calm meditation and a clear, steady inner vision.
intro: Purple tourmaline, often called siberite, is a violet to lilac variety of elbaite that looks like amethyst with an extra shimmer. The color can range from pale lavender to a deep, almost indigo purple, and good stones are strongly pleochroic, showing different shades of violet from different angles. Natural crystals form long, striated prisms, and faceted gems are bright and clean when well cut. It is far scarcer than amethyst or pink tourmaline, so many collectors treat it as a prize for a color-themed tourmaline set. In metaphysical circles it is loved as a more rarefied alternative to amethyst for meditation work.
history: The name siberite comes from Siberia, since the first purple tourmalines were found in the Ural Mountains of Russia, in the same pegmatites that gave tourmaline its early fame in the 19th century. Russian collectors and royal courts prized violet tourmaline among other Ural gems. Later, Brazil, Madagascar and Mozambique produced violet to lilac crystals from lithium-rich pegmatites. Because siberite appears as a trade and collector name rather than a separate mineral, folklore specific to it is thin, and its modern reputation draws on the older traditions of both amethyst and tourmaline. It has gained admirers among crystal lovers who want a rarer violet gem.
meaning: Crystal lore places purple tourmaline firmly in the Third Eye and Crown. Practitioners say it combines tourmaline's balancing quality with the spiritual touch of purple, making it a calm but alert meditation stone. It is thought to help you listen inward, whether to a hunch, a dream or a quiet sense of what is true. Because tourmaline is also seen as a stone that keeps energy balanced, many people feel it avoids the overstimulation some feel with very high-vibration stones. It is used by those who journal their dreams, practice divination or simply want to make quiet time at the end of a long day more intentional. Some call it a stone of dignity, for the poise it brings to a restless mind.
howToUse: Place a purple tourmaline on your forehead while lying down for a ten-minute meditation, or hold a crystal in your receiving hand while you ask a question and wait for the first quiet answer. Keep a small stone by your journal or under your pillow to support dream recall. Wear it as a pendant to keep intuition close during the day. For a grid, put it at the north point with amethyst and clear quartz. It is also a good altar companion for tarot or oracle readings, set beside the deck. Keep it out of strong sun when displaying it.
care: Purple tourmaline is hard and stable, but the color of violet stones can fade slowly in strong, long exposure to sunlight, so charge it by moonlight, not on a sunny sill. A brief rinse in lukewarm water and a soft cloth suffice for cleaning. Smoke, sound or a bed of clear quartz are good for cleansing. Avoid ultrasonic cleaners and rapid temperature changes, particularly with stones that have fractures. Store it in a pouch to keep it from scratching, and keep it away from harder gems.
identify: Genuine purple tourmaline is doubly refractive and shows pleochroism, with deeper color along the crystal's length. Natural crystals have lengthwise striations. Amethyst, purple sapphire, spinel and glass are the usual look-alikes, and amethyst lacks the striation and the strong color shift. Some violet tourmaline is heat-treated to improve color, and irradiation is possible in the trade. Because siberite is a trade name, ask the seller whether the stone is natural elbaite and request a lab report for expensive pieces.

faq.a: Siberite is the trade name for purple to violet tourmaline, a color variety of elbaite. The name refers to Siberia, where early violet crystals were found in the Ural pegmatites, though today most stones come from Brazil and Africa.

faq.q: What is purple tourmaline used for?
faq.a: Crystal practitioners use it for meditation, intuition and dream work. It is linked to the Third Eye and Crown chakras and is kept as a calming companion when you want to listen inward without feeling overwhelmed.

faq.q: Can purple tourmaline go in the sun?
faq.a: It is best not to. Violet tourmaline is generally hardy, but long exposure to strong sunlight can slowly fade the color. Charge it by moonlight or in gentle indirect light, and cleanse it with smoke or sound.
